catalog_quote: The mora is the tone bearing unit in Binumarien. High tone moras contrast with low tone moras. Every lexical item has at least and at most one high tone, so the system is obligatory and culminative. The Binumarien system lacks metricality: to my knowledge, there is no hierarchy of strong and weak syllables. ... I would argue that Binumarien distinguishes between high tone moras and toneless moras, which means the system is not binary, but privative. [p.17] ... new_statements.quote: The mora is the tone bearing unit in Binumarien. High tone moras contrast with low tone moras. Every lexical item has at least and at most one high tone, so the system is obligatory and culminative. The Binumarien system lacks metricality: to my knowledge, there is no hierarchy of strong and weak syllables. [p.17] ... Binumarien moras do not have a hierarchy of prominence either. The diacritic accent only marks a switch in tonal level. As I will demonstrate, the diacritic accent can occur two times, once, or not at all; in contrast to accent in stress-accent languages, where words have one and only one accented (metrically most prominent) syllable. [p.19]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Binumarien is a word-tone language: each word carries one of four melodies (H, LH, HL, LHL) with exactly one /H/ (privative H vs toneless), realised as level tones on moras, and the point(s) where the melody switches level are lexically specified and unpredictable. The author states there is no metrical structure and no hierarchy of prominence among moras/syllables, i.e. no word stress is described; the 'accent' used in the analysis is a purely diacritic tone-mapping mark, explicitly not stress-accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; no stress of any degree is posited.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged 'to my knowledge'; analysis restricted to nouns/NPs (verbs not analysed for tone). Utterance-level rules: every utterance must contain at least one H (default H on the utterance-final mora if no lexical H is realised) and downstep/declination lowers later H tones. Oatridge & Oatridge 1966 likewise describe only two-level register tone per mora and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tonal melodies established on nominal roots, affixed nouns and compounds (one melody per word; compounds take the first root's melody); citation forms and short NPs elicited in fieldwork 2018-19; utterance-level obligatory-H and downstep treated separately (3.4).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the single Binumarien speech community (autonym Afaqina; Oatridges worked at Onikuradarannai from 1959, van Dasselaar at Ubandeena 2018-19); no dialect split is reported; glottocode binu1245 / ISO bjr applies directly.

sources.note: Segmental phonemes plus suprasegmentals treated purely as tone: 'Binumarien has a system of register tones which show only two significant levels.. Each vowel is of one mora of length and carries its own register tone' (sec. 2.2, p.16-17); tone distribution restrictions (3.3). The word 'stress' does not occur; no statement on stress or accent placement.
